analysis.one_liner: Bans health insurers from denying coverage to children and young adults for pre-existing conditions.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it died in the Senate health committee after its 2009 introduction.
analysis.plain_summary: Senator Frank Lautenberg's bill would have made it illegal for group and individual health plans to deny coverage to anyone under 25 because of a pre-existing condition — a past illness, birth defect, or chronic condition that made the person costly to insure. Under the rules then in place, an insurer could refuse to pay for treatment of such conditions or impose long waiting periods. The bill was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Children and young adults under 25 with pre-existing health conditions — roughly 8 million children and young adults are uninsured at some point each year, and about 20% of school-aged children have a chronic illness, per the bill's own findings — along with their families, who would no longer face waiting periods or coverage limits when switching insurance.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Sick children and young adults under 25

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits group health plans and insurers in both the group and individual markets from imposing any pre-existing condition exclusion on anyone under 25.
Removes coverage limits and waiting periods that insurers could apply after a child had a 63-day gap in coverage, per the bill's findings.

The bill's findings note that state high-risk pools for people with pre-existing conditions were often underfunded, unaffordable, and had waiting lists, so this would have given families a direct route to private coverage instead.

The bill's findings state that pre-existing condition limits for children discourage families from leaving Medicaid or CHIP — implying the change could make private coverage a realistic option for families trying to move off public programs.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and employers sponsoring plans, who would bear the cost of covering previously excluded conditions for people under 25, with some of that cost likely spread into premiums for all enrollees. Union plans governed by pre-existing collective bargaining agreements got a delayed effective date.

drawbacks.text: The bill contains no mechanism to spread the added cost of covering pre-existing conditions, so premiums for other enrollees could rise — the standard insurance-industry objection to coverage mandates.
The protection is narrow: it covers only people under 25, leaving older adults with pre-existing conditions subject to the same exclusions the bill bans for children.
Coverage of sick enrollees who were previously uninsurable raises plans' costs, and insurers argued such mandates can push premiums up for everyone in the pool.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and targeted: children with serious conditions would gain access to care they were being denied, and families would stop losing coverage when they changed jobs or policies. The cost — higher premiums spread across insured pools — is genuine but modest relative to the protection, and the bill's own findings show the alternative (underfunded high-risk pools) was failing families. Its main design weakness is scope: it protects only the under-25 population rather than everyone.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate referred it to its health committee in March 2009, the committee never took it up, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Lautenberg introduced the bill with Senator Sherrod Brown and Senator Amy Klobuchar on March 19, 2009.
It was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day.
No further action — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — is recorded for the remainder of the 111th Congress.

The bill's stated goal — ending pre-existing condition denials for children — was later enacted on a broader basis as part of the major 2010 health care law, which banned pre-existing condition exclusions for all ages.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers are better off, since they avoided a new mandate to cover pre-existing conditions for children and young adults. Families with sick children gained nothing from this bill, though the same protection was later delivered through broader legislation.

for.name: Sen. Frank Lautenberg
for.role: U.S. Senator from New Jersey; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban pre-existing condition exclusions for people under 25.

for.name: Sens. Sherrod Brown and Amy Klobuchar
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors at introduction.

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral in March 2009 and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote; the bill died there.

against.name: Sen. Tom Harkin
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee of jurisdiction and never brought the bill up for consideration during the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No roll-call votes were ever taken; the bill's three Senate supporters were all Democrats or allied independents, and no Republican signed on, but no one ever voted against it on the record.

industries.note: The bill would have barred insurers in both group and individual markets from denying or delaying coverage of pre-existing conditions for anyone under 25, ending a cost-control practice at sick families' expense. Insurers escaped the mandate when the bill died.

Employer plans would have had to cover previously excluded conditions for workers' children, raising benefit costs, though healthier workforces can be easier to recruit and retain. Union plans got a delayed effective date under pre-existing collective bargaining agreements.
